title: Many children of Nepal’s Maoist war are done with politics - The Kathmandu Post
description: Many children of Nepal’s Maoist war are done with politics  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Agrani Chapagain grew up in prisons around eastern Nepal.

She was born in Biratnagar at the height of the Maoist insurgency. Her mother, Dharmashila Chapagain, was a Maoist cadre living in hiding. When Agrani was seven months old, police arrested her mother. The infant went with her into custody and eventually to prison.

As a child, she knew no other world. Guards, soldiers and fellow inmates were part of her everyday life. “We lived with other people in a cramped space,” she recalled to Kantipur recently.

Dharmashila was arrested in Biratnagar in late 2001. She was subsequently imprisoned in Morang, Sunsari, Jhapa and Ilam districts. Nepal was under a state of emergency, and Dharmashila remained under close surveillance even behind bars. “I was fortunate to have had my mother’s warmth and love,” Agrani said. “I was the youngest person there. The police, prison staff and other inmates all cared for me.”

She began school while her mother was being held at Ilam prison. She used to watch other children going to school from the prison gate. Her mother argued with the prison authorities until they let her enrol. “I carried a little lunchbox, and police officers took me to school and brought me back,” she recalled. “The other children called me ‘the prison girl’.”

Agrani said she also witnessed the brutal treatment of Maoist women in custody. “When we were at Ilam prison, I saw two women brought in, stripped and beaten on their first day,” she said. “They were so badly hurt they could barely stand or walk. I learnt later that my mother had been tortured in the same way.”

The Maoists launched their armed insurgency in February 1996, calling it the “People’s War”. Even as they fought the state, their cadres married and had children, often raising them in hiding and moving from one shelter to another. Some children, including Agrani, spent their earliest years in prison with their mothers. Most of them are now in their twenties, but few have followed their parents into politics. Many say the war is a past they would rather leave behind. Only a few have stuck to politics.

Ram Karki, former Maoist leader, sees three distinct paths among the children of the insurgency. “Some followed their parents into the movement but later earned a bad name,” he said. “Others experienced the hardships of war and have turned away from politics. Then there are some who want nothing to do with the conflict, or politics, anymore.”

***

Dharmashila was released on May 23, 2006, weeks after a mass uprising forced King Gyanendra Shah to end his direct rule and paved the way for Nepal’s peace process. For Agrani, who had spent much of her early childhood behind bars, freedom meant discovering a world she had known only from inside the prison walls.

“Only after my release did I realise how much of the world I had never known,” she said.

Agrani grew up without knowing her father. While she and her mother were in prison, security forces arrested Shankar Ghimire in Charali, Jhapa, and allegedly killed him in June 2002. Dharmashila learnt of his death while still behind bars, but Agrani would not learn the truth until much later.

Agrani believes the sacrifices made by her mother and others during the insurgency helped bring about political change in Nepal. Dharmashila was elected to the Constituent Assembly in 2008. She now divides her time between farming in Jhapa and political work. Agrani has since built a career in information technology. Based in Kathmandu, she works with IT companies in the United States and Australia. She resumed her education after Nepal’s peace process began in 2006, eventually completing secondary school and earning a degree in IT.

Having lost her father to the conflict and spent nearly five years in prison with her mother, Agrani has little interest in politics. “I want to pursue my career and support my mother financially,” she said.

Likewise, for Anunaya Acharya, 24, politics holds little appeal. She grew up in Liwang, Rolpa, a Maoist stronghold during the insurgency. But she is not drawn towards the political movement that shaped her childhood. Instead, the power struggles among political leaders have reinforced her view that politics is a dirty game. She is studying fashion design at IIFT School of Interior Nepal in Kathmandu. “I will probably start something of my own in fashion design,” she said.

Both her parents, Phanindra Acharya and Sunita Magar, were full-time Maoist cadres. When security forces began keeping a close watch on their home in Liwang, Phanindra went into hiding. He and Sunita married while he was on the run, crossing caste lines in a society where intercaste marriages have long faced resistance.

After Anunaya was born, her parents moved her between different places in Rolpa for two years to keep her safe. When she turned two, they left her with her paternal grandparents in Liwang. She grew up there. “My parents told me to do whatever I wanted. I chose not to go into politics,” she said.

Politics remains a part of Deepashikha’s family, but she wants nothing to do with it. She lost her grandfather, mother and paternal aunt during the insurgency, while her father and maternal uncle and aunt remain politically active. She has chosen a different path. “I see friends taking an interest in politics, but it has never appealed to me,” she said.

Deepashikha Nath was two when her mother, Pabitra Budha Magar, left her in the care of relatives in Kholagaun, in what is now Rukum West district, and travelled to Chaurjahari for party work in 1997. She was arrested there and later taken to a forest and allegedly shot dead.

Deepashikha’s father, Kal Bahadur Nath, was a commander in the Maoist People’s Liberation Army. She still remembers how her grandmother hid her from the police. “My grandmother would send us to the primary school in Phedikhola early each morning with sattu, a roasted flour mix, in our bags,” she recalled. “On school holidays, she would send us into the forest to hide. We were afraid the police would come looking for us and harm us. I remember Auntie Sunita Pariyar hiding us and giving us food. Sometimes we spent the night at her house.”

As a child, Deepashikha thought her mother had gone away for work and would one day come home. “I have so few memories of her that I try to piece together what she was like from photographs,” she said. “The war took my mother away, and I would rather not revisit those days.”

After completing a bachelor’s degree in business administration on a scholarship, Deepashikha found a job at an insurance company. “I’ve tried to move on, holding on to some memories and leaving the rest behind,” she said. “I don’t have any big ambitions.”

Shikha Sharma, who was born in Thabang, a Maoist stronghold in Rolpa, has also chosen to stay out of politics. She is studying for a bachelor’s degree in business studies in Ghorahi, Dang district.

Her parents, Bhumika Thapa Magar and Nabin Acharya, married while in hiding during the Maoist insurgency. “I was born in 2005, and my mother and I moved between different houses. It feels strange to think about it now,” Shikha said. “We returned to our home in Liwang after the peace process began in 2006. The transition was difficult at first, but things gradually got easier.”

Shikha sees the development of remote districts such as Rolpa and Rukum as one outcome of the war. “Rolpa has changed considerably since the war, with more hospitals, schools and roads,” she said. “The region could have progressed further if politics worked as it should.”

***

But not every child of Maoist insurgents is willing to leave it all behind.

Sandeep Pun, the son of a Maoist couple killed during the “People’s War”, remains active in politics. Sandeep was born in Musikot, Rukum. His parents, Surya Prakash Pun and Parampara Gautam, had been assigned by the party to work in Bajhang. They were allegedly killed by security forces in Bajhang in 2002, a week apart.

After their deaths, Sandeep was raised in several places, including Dang, Nepalgunj, Kapilvastu and Butwal, before being taken to Shimla in India. “I was five when I was taken to Kapilvastu,” he said. “People would flee whenever the army or police arrived, and Maoist fighters would turn up at night. For my safety, even my name was changed.”

In the March 2026 House of Representatives elections, Sandeep contested against Pushpa Kamal Dahal, coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party, in Rukum East. Sandeep stood for the Pragatisheel Loktantrik Party, which was formed by Janardan Sharma after he left the former Maoist party. The contest between two candidates with similar political backgrounds drew attention.

Sandeep Pun (front row, standing), the son of a Maoist couple killed during the ‘People’s War’, remains active in politics. He was born in Musikot, Rukum. Photo: Courtesy of Sandeep Pun

Sandeep believes Maoist leaders who took part in the insurgency later became politically and financially corrupt. “They gradually forgot their roots in the war,” he said.

Many joined the Maoist insurgency believing their sacrifices would lead to a better life. Sandeep says that promise has yet to be fulfilled for those who suffered through the war. “Neither the state nor the party has delivered on the promise of change to those who suffered during the war,” he said. “The leaders who fought in the insurgency lost touch with the very people and ideals they once represented.”

Sandeep said it was painful to see the children of Maoist fighters branded “terrorists” during the war. “Those who gave their lives lost everything, while others walked away with all the gains,” he said.

After the peace process began, Sandeep joined the Maoist-affiliated All Nepal National Independent Students’ Union-Revolutionary and eventually became its central vice-chair. He later left the party, disillusioned with its leadership. “The Maoists let down their honest leaders, cadres and supporters,” he said. “That’s why I left and joined another party.”

He lost to Dahal, receiving just 203 votes.

***

Former House speaker Onasari Gharti, now a Nepali Communist Party leader, says she is proud of having raised her children while continuing her work for the party during the insurgency. Gharti and fellow Maoist leader Barshaman Pun married while living in hiding during the insurgency. Their daughter, Shila, was born in Rolpa in 1998, and their son, Utsav, in Morang in 2003.

Maoist leaders depended on local communities to shelter them and help care for their children while they remained on the run during the war, Gharti said. “We relied on people for everything,” she said. “They gave us shelter and protection and helped raise our children. We had nothing of our own.”

According to Gharti, the party arranged for pregnant women and new mothers to be moved to safer areas. In some sensitive locations, the People’s Liberation Army provided security. Going to a hospital to give birth was often not an option.

Those living in hiding would usually stay in one house for no more than a week before moving to another hideout, she said.

Shila holds a master’s degree in economics, while Utsav has graduated in information technology. Both take an interest in politics but have stayed out of active political life.

There are no official figures for the number of children born to Maoist leaders and cadres living underground during the insurgency. A UNICEF assessment published in March 2016 estimated that between 52,000 and 57,000 children were affected by Nepal’s armed conflict between 1996 and 2003. During that period, state forces killed 155 children under the age of 17, while the Maoists were responsible for the deaths of 79 children.

The United Nations mission in Nepal verified that 2,973 people under the age of 18 had been recruited into the Maoist People’s Liberation Army. They were subsequently discharged from 27 temporary Maoist cantonments and reintegrated into civilian life. A February 2007 report by Human Rights Watch said more than 10,000 children had been displaced to avoid recruitment by the Maoists.

***

Karki, the former Maoist leader, said the lack of any organised system for educating or politically orienting children born while their parents were in hiding may also explain their limited interest in politics.

Sociologist Samjhana Wagle Bhattarai said children who were born and raised in conflict zones had a different understanding of society, its hardships, social values and conflicts from those who grew up in peacetime. Many of them may also have turned away from politics as their parents’ party splintered and drifted from its founding ideology, she said.

title: Eight injured in fire at steel factory in Banke - The Rising Nepal
description: Eight injured in fire at steel factory in Banke  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Our Correspondent,Bara, Nov. 2: Eight persons were injured when a fire broke out at Ambe Steel Rod Factory in Bakaspur of Janaki Rural Municipality-5, Banke, on Sunday morning.

The fire broke out at around 5:40 am after an electrical short circuit occurred in three furnaces used for melting iron, each with a capacity of 25 tonnes.

Of the injured, five are from Banke and three are from Bahraich district in India. They were initially taken to Bheri Hospital in Nepalgunj for treatment. Two of them were later referred to Lucknow, India, for further treatment, according to a news bulletin of the Police Headquarters.

The injured have been identified as Shiva Prasad Chamar, 28, Ramdin Harijan, 22, Prem Dhobi, 24, Dilip Kumar Yadav, 29, and Laxmi Ram Yadav, 35, all residents of Janaki Rural Municipality-5, Banke.

The other three injured are Raj Kumar Nishad, 29, Nashib Kumar Nishad, 24, and Binod Kumar Nishad, 25, all residents of Kathautiya in Bahraich district, India.

According to police, a five-member team led by Senior Police Sub-Inspector Ludra Bahadur KC from the Khajura Khurd Area Police Office was dispatched to the site immediately after receiving information about the fire.

With the help of two fire engines from Nepalgunj Sub-Metropolitan City and one from Kohalpur Municipality, along with personnel from Nepal Police, the Armed Police Force and local residents, the fire was completely brought under control at 8:15 am.

At 8:45 am, Shiva Prasad Chamar and Ramdin Harijan were referred to Lucknow, India, for further treatment.

Details of the other losses caused by the fire are yet to be ascertained.

title: Nepal plans micronutrient survey in December — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal plans micronutrient survey in December — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal plans to conduct a nationwide survey in December to assess the population’s status regarding vitamin A, iron, folic acid and iodine, as well as the prevalence of anemia. The survey will begin six weeks after a campaign to provide children with vitamin A and deworming medicines, the Kathmandu Post reports.

The campaign is scheduled for November 3 and 4. About 2.1 million children aged six to 59 months are expected to receive vitamin A, while around 1.9 million children aged one to five will also receive deworming tablets. About 54,000 female community health volunteers have been enlisted across the country to carry it out.

Funding and objectives of the survey

Previously, officials considered postponing the regular campaign until March next year in order to assess the prevalence of vitamin A deficiency without prior supplementation. However, expert groups, including those involving the World Health Organization and UNICEF, advised against delaying the program, as children’s nutritional status should not worsen for the sake of the survey.

The previous national micronutrient survey in Nepal was conducted in 2016 with U.S. financial support. Such surveys are usually carried out once every ten years. The new survey was initially planned for May-June, but was suspended indefinitely after the Donald Trump administration froze U.S. aid worldwide.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

According to officials, Washington, at the initiative of the U.S. Embassy in Nepal, decided to provide UNICEF with $3.5 million to conduct the survey. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are expected to provide technical assistance. The report may affect future national nutrition policy.

Review of iodized salt policy

According to officials, the survey results may be used to review mass vitamin A supplementation programs, the targeted distribution of micronutrient powders, salt iodization and the promotion of a more diverse diet. After receiving the report, the authorities will also have to decide whether to reduce the iodine content in salt.

Nepal’s Salt Trading Corporation adds iodine to salt at a concentration of 50 parts per million, while the WHO recommends between 15 and 40 parts per million. The 2016 survey showed that 68% of the country’s population consumes iodine in amounts significantly exceeding the recommended level. Doctors suspect that the high iodine content in salt may be one of the factors behind the prevalence of thyroid diseases and hypertension.

title: Nepal allocates 43 million rupees for Marsi rice cultivation — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal allocates 43 million rupees for Marsi rice cultivation — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal’s Karnali Province has allocated 43 million Nepalese rupees this year for the cultivation and marketing of local Marsi rice. Demand for this reddish-brown aromatic rice is growing in Nepalese cities and abroad, but the spread of plant diseases and rising costs are complicating its cultivation. As the Kathmandu Post reports, agricultural specialists are recording a decline in production due to crop damage.

Marsi rice is cultivated on 5,280 hectares in Karnali Province, and its production totaled 9,725 tonnes last year. The largest area is in Jumla district—2,888 hectares, where 6,125 tonnes were harvested last year. In Mugu and Humla, the crop was grown on 1,060 and 1,340 hectares, respectively.

Demand outpaces supply

Farmers in Jumla, Mugu and Humla receive orders for paddy rice and processed rice even before the harvest is completed. In Jumla, traders offer about 180 rupees per kilogram of paddy rice, while Marsi rice sells for 250–300 rupees per kilogram in Kathmandu.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Harikrishna Bhandari, owner of the Karnali Organic Shop in Kathmandu, said he sold 15 tonnes of Marsi rice last year, three tonnes of which were exported to Japan, South Korea, the United States and the United Kingdom. The Chandannath Multipurpose Cooperative supplies rice, including to Kathmandu, Pokhara, Chitwan, Biratnagar and Dharan. According to its representative Rishiram Pandey, the product can cost up to 2,000 rupees per kilogram on international markets.

Diseases and crop insurance

Agricultural specialists note that over the past two to three years, crops have been affected by neck blast caused by the fungus Magnaporthe grisea. The disease damages the above-ground parts of the plant, reduces production and worsens grain quality. According to farmers, costs are also rising due to the purchase of seeds and fertilizers and the need for weeding, while hail destroyed crops on some farms last year.

Insurance companies began offering insurance for Marsi crops in Jumla in 2022 through the district agricultural development office. According to its data, after a state subsidy, the insurance premium is 50 rupees per ropani—a local unit of area equal to approximately 509 square meters. The ministry also said it had spent a total of 130 million rupees on the cultivation and promotion of Marsi rice and designated 17 local communities in three districts as production zones.

title: Desmond Macgcnaimhshi, 1941-2026 - Nepali Times
description: Desmond Macgcnaimhshi, 1941-2026  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The Irish bard, Desmond Macgcnaimhshi, a music legend for 36 years, passed away on 24 October on Kimdol Hill at the foot of sacred Swayambhunath in Kathmandu.

With his long grey ponytail and abundant moustache, Desmond played his last set at Ramsterdam in Boudha just five days previously as he had for the past 15 years, bringing joy to friends and audience.

I met Des as we called him, in the 1990s. We had much in common, both being 60s dropouts and traveling the world. Except I came over the Pacific, leaving corporate America after finishing a military stint.

Desmond was born in the Gaeltacht, a region of Ireland impoverished since the potato famine in the nineteenth century. It’s ‘where only bad and nothing good happens’ but also where inhabitants learn the art of sharpening their wit on trouble.

Desmond was part of the Dublin rock and roll scene in the early 1960s, playing with a band called The Caravelles. He joined the merchant marines as a painter and then jumped ship at the first interesting port, which was Morocco.

He never looked back, living his life in many countries wherever he felt a connection to the earth and spirit worlds and could play music. He chose Kathmandu as his long, last chapter.

In 1974 he met and married Joan Jacobs, the love of his life, and they resided in Sri Lanka, Goa, and other parts of India. When they moved to Kathmandu in the late 1990s they saw the valley as their spiritual home, appreciating Buddhist teachings and feeling surrounded by a sense of the sacred.

He opened a recording studio in Kimdol below Swayambhu and played with many bands like Too Loose to Trek, Phil’n the Blanks, and Usual Suspects. He also played regularly at The Irish Pub, Upstairs, Spam’s, and New Orleans. He was instrumental in launching Ramsterdam as a happening place on Mahankal Road in Boudha.

Sometimes his musician pal, Beppe, would come in from Italy to play with him. Desmond also visited his friend on Elba Island, where they toured and were requested to perform every evening, playing 45 gigs in two months, much to Desmond’s delight. They also recorded some of Des’ original music at Beppe’s recording studio.

Des wrote much of his repertoire himself. While he played a fine Mr Bojangles and Delta Blues music from the southern US, he preferred to play his own works and sometimes made that clear.

His songs reflected his travels, a heart that had known love, and encounters with dilemmas and suffering, all tempered with Irish soul and wit and buoyed by masterful music on his guitar.

“You don’t find the song – it finds you someday,” he would say. As it goes with the blues, some of his pieces drew on people lost and forgotten by others.

‘Can’t even give it away’ recalled a glimpse of a prostitute in Italy, her looks on the wane, trying and failing to get business along a highway outside of town, but held kindly in Des’ eye. He also often reminded us that the Irish were the first slaves of the world “and don’t forget that!”

For thirty years Desmond escaped the winters of Kathmandu by traveling to Koh Payam, an island in Thailand, and playing in another music scene that he had helped to create. International musicians gather there for the winter, playing an open mic format every night, moving from venue to venue across the island. I visited his scene last year and found that Desmond is revered there as well.

INSPIRATION

Des had a growing following of young Nepalis who were inspired by his mastery of acoustic guitar and the authenticity of his songs. At the Friday night gigs at Ramsterdam, he was often joined by the owner’s son, Benjamin, who graduated from being Desmond’s student to sharing the stage with him.

These rock and roll artists could get the crowds to leave their chairs and hit the floor dancing. Whether with acoustic or amplified music, an evening with Desmond became infused with joy.

I grew up with Italian Americans who carried on about not liking the Irish, which was based on the Irish having reached America first and taken all the good jobs. But I was immediately drawn to this Irishman with mischief in his mouth and a sparkle in his eyes.

We both liked to raise up mischief, while keeping an eye out for meaning. For the past 10 years we would meet up with a posse of friends every Saturday at the farmers market to address the world’s problems - for which we made great headway, in intention.

Desmond could talk learnedly and humorously about anything from affairs of state, books, or the music world. His presence enlivened the table. As shared by a friend: “Even if he was trying to convince you of the worst possible outcome of any situation you or he were contemplating, which was his pessimistic inclination, he would conclude by laughing at his gloomy self.” And we would all laugh too and feel better about the world than when we started.

Desmond Macgcnaimhshi was one of the last remaining 1970s ‘hippy trail’ expats who utterly cut his own path in life. He lived and died as he chose, playing music throughout his 85 years and passing away in his sleep on his beloved Kimdol Hill.

Bon Voyage, my friend, we will miss you dearly. May you pass through the next Bardol unhindered by obstacles. Svaha: may it be so.

When your rooster crows at the break of dawn

Look out your window and I’ll be gone

You’re the reason I’m a-traveling on

title: Right Or Wrong, Rightists Gain - The Rising Nepal
description: Right Or Wrong, Rightists Gain  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
China’s effective resilience, Russia’s strategic silence, North Korea's longstanding obstinacy and Iranian insistence on noninterference combine to form a formidable force against the US-led Western world as well as Asia-Pacific nations like Australia, Japan and South Korea. Others are less worried, as they see the prospects of credible choices in making instead of being ceaselessly dominated as in the eight decades-plus after the Second World War.

Australian government in 2025 offered a US$12,000 relocation bonus to the people of the island of Kiwis willing to shift to Queensland, where there are “warmer days and higher pay”. The same offer does not flash at the hundreds of millions from non-White majority nations. New Zealand’s population of 5.3 million, already a highly sparsely populated country of nearly the combined size of Nepal and Bangladesh, is home to one of the largest diasporas in the organisation for the Paris-headquartered Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), a club of mostly rich countries.

The billion-dollar note of interest is that the land of kangaroos does not extend a similar invite to people of other countries, who are not of “European”, American or Canadian descent. Although one would refrain from calling the policy racist, it does sound intriguing. New Zealand is almost twice the size of Nepal, with less than one-fifth of the South Asian landlocked country’s population of nearly thirty million.

How do you mix or match merit and identity? It might be attractive to many at the first sound and sight of the word “representation”, but it engages considerable energy and entails a balancing act between quality participation and technical representation. Regime change has become a major American export inspired not by any “liberal” manifestation, but sheer ulterior motive garbed in “vital interests” and “popular demand”.

US President Barack Obama and Joe Biden, vice president under the country’s first black president, stressed discrimination, citing past faults to override merit in selection, which created political division. In contrast, Biden’s immediate predecessor and successor, Donald Trump, continues a war against diversity, equality and inclusion policies. The Department of Education directed schools against the use of race as criteria for staff employment, awarding scholarships and treating students “differently”.

Power equation

Europe produces little of its required resources and sizeable sections of the continent’s population have nostalgia for their colonial legacy that has become not just irrelevant but grim. Others are breaking free from their long slumber to realise that their security base and steady supply of vital natural resources and raw materials are witnessing noticeable depletion. Replenishment is a challenge not because of a shortage in international reserves but because of the weaponisation of the same by rivals emerging with undertaking missions of their own, which the traditional powers receive as a direct menace to their hegemony.

Others among middle-level powers are also beginning to conclude that the future is with the East and not with Europe any longer. With space for opportunities found to be shrinking, talk of a free market of virtually unbridled nature is reduced to a whisper. Liberal migration policy is no longer a norm, substituted by strict to stringent measures. The general policy is to give entry to only the best and the brightest who meet the host’s shortage of special hands.

The tendency would intensify with the passage of each year; the argument—if it came to that point at all—would be “to address our national interest and serve our people”. Until the recent past, such loud talk, not to speak of actual action, would have attracted condemnation as “outright rightist” thinking. In other words, the vilification campaign would be close to calling it a “pariah” attitude.

Times are changing for slogans and rhetoric to be reset to suit immediate expediency, which underscores how the ostensible faith in and commitment to long-floated ideas are trampled without qualms when the crunch comes. France, the land where the lofty idea of “equality, liberty and fraternity” first echoed during the 1789 Revolution that guillotined some 17,000 men and women of all classes, irrespective of class or creed, has made no bones about its interpretation of social norms and public display of religious faith. Complaints are made about Muslim-related books in school and public libraries being sternly scrutinised.

Case in point

In one of such recent measure, the French government’s move to ban a major four-day annual Muslim gathering planned in the outskirts of central Paris at the pretext of “security threat”, it suffered a setback. A court verdict overturned the order to prevent the planned programme from being held. The capital city’s police vainly tried to convince the court that the annual Muslim event could be a target of terrorists or risk clashing with demonstrations by opposing groups. The bench did not buy the argument and provided relief to the organisers just two hours before the scheduled programme.

The French government is at the forefront among European Union members in planning a new “anti-separatism” law that targets Muslim organisations seen as engaged in ideas and activities that contravene the country’s basic interpretation of national integrity and security. Had such an argument come from ideological opponents or economic competitors away from the European continent, it would have been reviled as “ultranationalist” and even “undemocratic”, if not “anti-people” altogether.

Since the onset of the 2020s, the rightist movement in Europe—and the US—has gathered momentum. Britain’s UK Reform and Germany’s Alternative for Deutschland are not the only political parties gaining political ground and the weightage that goes with it. The Dutch Party for Freedom and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy are in the same league. Spain and Portugal are witnessing the gradual rise of right-wing populist parties. Without a doubt, rightists and populists have a field day in the ongoing campaigns for political shakeups in Asia and Europe. Africa could be next, if military brass does not do its act as an excuse for busying in action.





(Professor Kharel specialises in political communication.)

title: 7,688 disaster incidents recorded across Nepal between mid-April and Nov 1 - Khabarhub
description: 7,688 disaster incidents recorded across Nepal between mid-April and Nov 1  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: A total of 7,688 disaster incidents were recorded across Nepal between mid-April and November 1, claiming 402 lives and leaving 17 people missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The Authority has documented various types of disasters during the period, including snakebites, landslides, floods, lightning strikes, fires, lake-related incidents, animal attacks, avalanches, storms, heavy rainfall, boat capsizings, forest fires, explosions, hailstorms and earthquakes.

Ram Bahadur KC, spokesperson and deputy secretary of the Authority, said the country recorded 1,735 landslides, 1,668 snakebite incidents, 1,641 fires, 593 heavy rainfall events, 537 storms, 466 floods, 417 animal attacks and 333 lightning incidents.

Similarly, the records include 192 forest fires, 79 lake-related incidents, six avalanches, nine earthquakes, four hailstorms, two boat capsizings, one explosion and five other incidents.

Of the 402 fatalities, 116 were caused by snakebites, 77 by landslides, 41 by floods, 36 by lightning strikes, 32 by fires, 27 by lake-related incidents, 23 by animal attacks, 19 by avalanches, 16 by storms, seven by heavy rainfall, five by boat capsizings, one by a forest fire, one by an explosion and five by other incidents.

According to the Authority, 2,529 people have been injured and 9,857 families displaced by the disasters during the reporting period.

The Authority also stated that the detailed damage assessment of the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa on August 26 has not yet been entered into its information system. Therefore, the impact of that disaster is not reflected in the current statistics.

title: First step: Editorial on Nepal floods and the promise of FRLD aid - Telegraph India
description: First step: Editorial on Nepal floods and the promise of FRLD aid  Telegraph India
publisher.title: Telegraph India
full_article:
The devastating floods that struck Nepal's Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river basins in August rank among the country's worst catastrophes. The disaster killed more than 1,500 people, damaged critical infrastructure, and left thousands homeless and missing. Facing the enormous task of rebuilding community lives and livelihoods, Nepal sought compensation from the United Nations' Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage — a multilateral climate finance mechanism under the aegis of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) meant to assist developing nations crippled by disasters brought about by climate change. It must be noted that the FRLD was set up after a prolonged struggle by developing countries to secure financial assistance for climate-induced destruction that can no longer be prevented through mitigation or adaptation. The FRLD has now provisionally set aside $21.6 million for Nepal, marking the first time that the fund has been used for a country-specific disaster. This is a welcome step towards climate accountability. After all, Nepal’s contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions is negligible. Yet the nation, much like other countries in the Global South as well as island states, is paying a shockingly disproportionate price at the sacrificial altar of climate change.

However, FRLD is far from a perfect aid mechanism. The Nepalese government, for instance, estimates the total loss and damage from the floods to be at $2.7 billion while recovery needs stand at $4.77 billion. The allocation thus covers less than 0.5% of Nepal's requirements. The yawning gap between funding and the scale of destruction reveals one of the persistent challenges of climate financing templates. Moreover, the earmarking of funds does not mean that the money reaches adversely affected communities on time. Nepal submitted its request in August, but the fund’s board convened a meeting only in October. Procedural requirements lead to delays in disbursement. Such delays extract a heavy price. But these limitations do not undermine the need for climate finance models. The long-standing commitment by wealthy nations to mobilise $100 billion annually in climate finance by 2020 has been contested over its adequacy and delivery. The FRLD contains only a fraction of the money major greenhouse gas emitters have pledged to contribute. There is a case for the Global South to press for a permanent rapid-response mechanism, transparent allocation criteria, and direct access to aid for affected countries. Can regional blocs and financial institutions step in? The exploration of alternative sources of climate finance, however, must not absolve wealthy nations of their commitments.

title: Land subdivision halted in 333 local units in Nepal — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Land subdivision halted in 333 local units in Nepal — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the subdivision of land plots into smaller parcels has been suspended in 333 local units that have not completed land classification by use. The federal government is preparing the fourth amendment to the 2022 Land Use Regulations to ease the restrictions, The Kathmandu Post reports.

Ganesh Prasad Bhatta, spokesperson for the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, said that the draft amendment has already been sent to the Ministry of Finance for approval. After receiving approval, it is to be sent to the Ministry of Law, while the changes will take effect only after approval by the Cabinet of Ministers.

Classification completed by 420 units

Under the 2019 Land Use Act, local land use councils must classify land and ensure the implementation of relevant policy based on maps and data provided by the government. Land must be divided into ten categories, including agricultural, residential, industrial, forest, mining and commercial areas.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

So far, only 420 local units have completed the classification. They have determined land use designations for ten types of use, including agriculture, industry and residential development. The sale of entire plots, the division of property among family members, transfers pursuant to court decisions and corrections to land records remain permitted.

Restrictions imposed repeatedly

The government has already amended the rules several times, temporarily allowing plot subdivision in local units where classification has not been completed. At the same time, after missed deadlines, the restrictions were reinstated each time. In August 2026, plot subdivision was halted in 390 local units, and in 2025, in 500. In September 2024, restrictions on land administrative services were in force in 620 units.

The ministry reported that 176 local units had prepared data at the level of individual land plots, while another 130 had defined the necessary criteria and updated maps. Bhim Prasad Dhungana, a representative of the Municipal Association of Nepal, said that many communities lack funds and technical specialists: carrying out the work costs at least 1.5 million to 2 million rupees. The Office of the Auditor General also called for providing local authorities with the necessary resources and coordinating classification with the Department of Survey.

title: Nepal’s ruling party will not support Thapa as ambassador to Japan — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal’s ruling party will not support Thapa as ambassador to Japan — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
The leadership of Nepal’s ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party has agreed not to support the appointment of Jigyan Kumar Thapa as the country’s ambassador to Japan. The reason cited was a potential conflict of interest related to the Japanese permanent resident status of his family members, financial obligations and other ties to that country, Kathmandu Post reports.

According to the publication, this understanding was reached during a meeting between party chair Rabi Lamichhane and Prime Minister Balendra Shah. A source close to the head of government said Thapa could be considered for a diplomatic post in another country, but the party would not support his candidacy specifically for work in Japan.

Proposal to withdraw candidacy

The party leadership also discussed the possibility of proposing that Thapa withdraw his candidacy in exchange for assurances that he could later be considered for another diplomatic appointment. At the same time, the final decision on withdrawal must be made by the candidate himself.

The parliamentary hearing committee has already recommended that Thapa withdraw from the nomination. Committee chair Bodh Narayan Shrestha, secretary Tul Bahadur Kandel and lawmakers from the Rastriya Swatantra Party separately asked him about such a decision. According to committee members, Thapa replied that he would think about it but has not yet given a final answer.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Review of ties to Japan

During the hearings, lawmakers asked Thapa about his permanent resident status, financial obligations and previous work at Japanese institutions. He told the committee that he gave up his Japanese permanent residence permit in March in connection with his nomination for ambassador. At the same time, his wife and sons retain Japanese permanent resident status.

The committee twice asked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to obtain information from the Japanese side about Thapa’s status, his possible outstanding financial obligations and potential payments from Japanese public funds. Japanese authorities refused to disclose the data, citing privacy protection. The ministry informed the committee that it had not received documentary confirmation that Thapa had renounced permanent residence in Japan.

The government recommended ambassadorial candidates for 13 countries on September 18, and they were registered with the parliamentary committee on September 23. The deadline for reviewing Thapa’s candidacy expires on November 5.
